extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers, and scholarly publishers concerned with research integrity and retraction policy
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial commentary on the causes, metrics, policy gaps, and consequences of scientific article retractions in biomedical and life-science publishing, with recommendations for journal-level transparency and detection practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of retraction — author misconduct (fraud, duplications, plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the >2000 retracted biomedical and life-science articles studied, nearly 70% were retracted due to author misconduct, with the most common problem being suspected fraud (43.4%), followed by duplications and plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misconduct-related retractions have risen substantially (≈10-fold since 1975). Although misconduct-related retractions are a small fraction of total publications, their rising number is the primary concern. Use these cause categories when classifying retractions and prioritizing detection efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices should be clear and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Published retraction notices are often vague and unclear as to the cause of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague notices hinder accurate counts and understanding of retraction causes and likely lead to underestimation of misconduct. Journals should aim for clear, specific retraction notices that state reason(s) for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of retractions with journal Impact Factor (IF)
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a direct correlation between Impact Factor (IF) and retraction numbers; prestigious journals (e.g., Science, PNAS, Nature) have the most retracted articles, while many lower-IF journals had few or none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher visibility/IF increases both the likelihood of detecting/reporting misconduct and the potential reward for notoriety; editors and reviewers at high-IF journals should be especially vigilant about detecting fraud and duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to initiate retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions are generally initiated by journal editors, but some editors may be reluctant to accept that a fraudulent article was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial willingness to investigate and, when warranted, retract is essential. Reluctance to retract leads to persistent fraudulent literature and undercounting of retractions; policies and procedures should empower editors to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retracted articles can continue to be cited and may boost notoriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracted articles often continue to be cited; infamous articles may be quoted more often than 'famous' ones and can contribute to impact metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and indexing services should ensure retraction status is clearly linked to the article record to reduce post-retraction citation. Editors should be aware that retracted work can remain influential if not clearly flagged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction index as a metric for journal-level retraction rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction index: number of retractions per journal (over a period) divided by the total number of articles appearing on PubMed in that period, multiplied by 1000 to yield whole numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a standardized measure to compare journals' retraction frequency; because raw retraction counts are small, scaling (×1000) makes comparisons easier. Use cautiously—higher index may reflect better detection/reporting as well as higher misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency index components for journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed transparency index elements include: the article review protocol of the journal, whether underlying data are made available, whether the journal uses plagiarism-detection software, whether a mechanism for dealing with fraud issues exists, and whether corrections and retractions are as clear as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should consider adopting these transparency elements (AJNR examples noted: review protocol, plagiarism detection, policy on duplication/fraud). A transparency index can help readers evaluate journal practices on integrity and error correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal retraction policies should exist and be publicly stated
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of 122 high-IF biomedical journals found 62% did not have a formal policy regarding retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should adopt, document, and publicize formal retraction/correction policies (AJNR provides an example). Lack of formal policy correlates with inconsistent handling of suspected misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of retraction — aim for rapid correction
rubrics_metrics.description: More recent data show the system is faster: nearly 50% of retractions occur within 2 years postpublication and this delay seems to be shortening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faster detection and retraction reduces the period during which fraudulent findings influence the literature. Journals and institutions should aim to expedite investigations and corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study features that increase likelihood of false findings (higher scrutiny criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics associated with eventual false findings include: small populations, small overall effects, financial interests, and work in a 'hotter' field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers and editors should apply heightened scrutiny to studies with these features; such studies are at greater risk of distortion, selective reporting, or being later retracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication screening can detect fraud (including 'article in press')
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud is sometimes detected even at the preliminary submission or 'in press' stage; retractions have occurred for articles not yet assigned issue/pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement submission-stage checks (plagiarism detection, data availability checks, methodological plausibility checks) because fraud can be identified prior to final publication. Be transparent when withdrawal reasons involve suspected misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigation and consequences for large-scale fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases (e.g., Stapel, Fujii) show that institutional panels can find large numbers of fabricated publications and lead to formal investigations, retractions, and scrutiny of funding misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should coordinate with institutions for investigation when large-scale fabrication is suspected; institutions must have processes to investigate and report findings to enable retraction and correction of the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retracted articles' citation trajectory — short-term high citation, long-term decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracted articles were likely to be highly cited in their first year, but citations for retractions were down ~72% by 10 years; in one study, retracted articles accumulated many citations and retractions were acknowledged in only 6.4%–7.7% of citing journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because retracted work can have strong early influence, rapid and visible retraction notices (and notification to indexers) are critical to reduce long-term propagation; journals should track and, where possible, notify citing authors or issue notices in linked systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of admitted fabrication/falsification underscores need for oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey data: ~2% of academics admitted to falsifying or fabricating data and 28% claimed to know colleagues who had done it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prevalence estimates support robust ethics oversight, routine screening, and institutional/journal-level safeguards rather than assuming misconduct is vanishingly rare.
